title: Wildlands visitor predictor
blurb: Built with a team (we called ourselves Procyon) for Wildlands zoo. Uses machine learning on weather and event data to forecast how busy the park will be on a given day.
detail: Built with a team for Wildlands, a zoo. Our team name was Procyon. A Flask dashboard predicts daily visitor numbers using machine learning, LightGBM models trained on weather, event, and historical visitor data. Includes a login system, a 365-day forecast, and sliders to test different scenarios. Deployed with Docker.

title: Mort & Sebastiaan
blurb: Built this robot twice with a team on Arduino: Mort solved a physical maze, Sebastiaan followed a line and used a gripper to place an object on a target. We won with Sebastiaan.
detail: A competition robot I built with a team, twice, on Arduino. The first version, Mort, had to solve a physical maze, its code lives on a branch called Physical-Maze in a teammate's repo. The second, Sebastiaan, is a line follower: it follows a line using light sensors, uses a distance sensor to start once a flag is lifted, picks up an object with a gripper, steers around obstacles, and drops the object on a target square at the end. We won with Sebastiaan.

title: Chess Robot
blurb: Watches a chessboard with a camera, works out the position, and plays a move back.
detail: A robot that watches a chessboard through a camera, works out the position with machine vision, and plays a move against a human opponent. Involved bridging Python and C, a lot of 3D-printed parts, and learning Linux along the way.

title: frogpet
blurb: A tiny frog that lives on your desktop, notices which app you're using, and comments on it with a local LLM.
detail: A desktop pet built with Python and Tkinter. A little frog walks around your screen, notices which application is focused, and reacts with speech-bubble commentary generated by a local LLM through Ollama. Mostly an excuse to mess with window tracking and prompt design.

title: Smart Liquid Dispenser
blurb: Built with Sven and Lennon. Pumps a set amount of liquid with a peristaltic pump, and a load cell checks the weight actually matches.
detail: Group project with Sven and Lennon. A Raspberry Pi controls a peristaltic pump to dispense a set number of milliliters of liquid, and a load cell (HX711) checks the actual weight against the target so it can correct itself.

title: Fishsee
blurb: An aquarium monitor built with a friend. Tracks temperature, pH, turbidity, and flow, and manages a pump and an LED strip.
detail: Built with a friend for an Arduino Uno R4. Reads temperature, pH, turbidity, and flow sensors, drives a pump and servos, and controls an addressable LED strip. Uses a Raspberry Pi over a serial connection to handle heavier data requests so the Arduino doesn't run out of memory.
